info.name: OpenAI Playground — Chat Completions vs Responses API
info.description:
# OpenAI API playground

Built to mirror the two APIs behind this repo's DoctorAssistant bots (CLAUDE.md 3.9 and 3.10) so you can poke at them by hand.

## Setup (one minute)

1. Open the collection's **Variables** tab.
2. Replace `api_key`'s CURRENT VALUE with your real key (`sk-...`). Leave the initial value as the placeholder so you never commit a key.
3. Send **3.1 List models**. A 200 means you are ready.

## Suggested order

`3.1` → `1.1` → `1.2` (turn knobs) → `1.6`+`1.7` (tool loop, manual history) → `2.1` → `2.2`+`2.3` (chaining) → `2.5`+`2.6` (tool loop, chained) → `2.4` (structured output) → `2.7` (streaming) → `2.10` (read the chain back).

Requests 2.3, 2.6, 2.9-2.11 and 1.7 depend on variables captured by an earlier request's test script — run the request they name first. Open Postman's **Console** (⌥⌘C) to see the captured ids, the reply text and the token counts logged for every call.

## The one-line difference

Chat Completions is stateless — you resend the whole conversation, so input tokens grow every turn. Responses is chained — you send a pointer, and they do not.

Full parameter reference: `docs/openai-postman-guide.md` in this repo.

item.name: 1 · Chat Completions API  (/v1/chat/completions)
item.description:
The older, message-array API. You resend the WHOLE conversation every call — there is no server-side chaining here. Everything is under `messages`.

Read `docs/openai-postman-guide.md` in this repo for the full parameter guide.

request.description:
The smallest legal request: a model and one user message.

**Things to try**
- Change `model` to a bigger/smaller one and watch `usage` + latency.
- Add a second object to `messages` with `"role": "assistant"` to fake prior context.

**Where the answer is:** `choices[0].message.content`.
**Where the cost is:** `usage.prompt_tokens` / `usage.completion_tokens`.

Every commonly-used sampling parameter set explicitly so you can turn them one at a time.

| Param | Range | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `temperature` | 0–2 | Randomness. 0 ≈ deterministic. Above ~1.2 gets incoherent. |
| `top_p` | 0–1 | Nucleus sampling: only consider tokens in the top P probability mass. **Change this OR temperature, not both.** |
| `max_completion_tokens` | int | Hard cap on the reply. Hitting it gives `finish_reason: "length"` — a truncated, not shorter, answer. |
| `n` | int | Generate N independent replies. Bills for all N. |
| `stop` | array | Up to 4 strings; generation halts before them (they are not returned). |
| `presence_penalty` | -2–2 | Positive = push toward NEW topics. |
| `frequency_penalty` | -2–2 | Positive = punish repeating the same token. |
| `seed` | int | Best-effort reproducibility with fixed temperature. Compare `system_fingerprint` across runs. |
| `user` | string | Your own end-user id, for abuse tracing. |

**Experiment:** set `temperature: 0` and send twice — near-identical. Set `2` and send twice — wildly different.

Chat Completions is **stateless**. Memory exists only because you resend it.

Note the shape: `system` → `user` → `assistant` → `user`. Every turn you append two more objects and resend the lot, so input tokens grow linearly with conversation length.

This is exactly the cost curve the Responses API's `previous_response_id` avoids — compare with request 2.3.

`stream: true` turns the response into Server-Sent Events. Postman shows the raw `data: {...}` lines; each chunk carries `choices[0].delta.content` (a fragment, not the whole reply).

`stream_options.include_usage: true` appends a FINAL chunk carrying `usage` — without it, streaming gives you no token counts at all. That matters if you are logging cost (your `bot_token_usage` table does).

The stream ends with a literal `data: [DONE]` line, which is not JSON — parsers must skip it.

Forces the reply to satisfy a JSON schema. This is the same `BotDecision` shape your Version 1 bot uses (`bot/promptstuffing/BotDecision.java`).

**Strict-mode rules — all three or it 400s:**
1. `additionalProperties: false` on every object.
2. EVERY property listed in `required` — optionality is expressed as `"type": ["string", "null"]`, not by omitting the key.
3. `strict: true`.

The result still arrives as a **string** in `choices[0].message.content` — you parse it yourself.

**Try breaking it:** delete `additionalProperties` and resend to see the exact 400.

Your five real clinic tools, in Chat Completions' **nested** format (`{type, function: {name, description, parameters}}`) — note the Responses API flattens this.

**What comes back:** `finish_reason: "tool_calls"` and `choices[0].message.tool_calls[]`, each with an `id` and `function.arguments` (a JSON **string**).
The model has NOT answered yet — it asked a question.

`tool_choice` options: `"auto"` (default), `"none"`, `"required"` (must call something), or `{"type":"function","function":{"name":"get_available_slots"}}` to force one.
`parallel_tool_calls: false` forces one call at a time — easier to follow while learning.

The test script saves `tool_call_id` for request 1.7.

Run 1.6 first — `{{tool_call_id}}` is filled in automatically by its test script.

You must resend the whole history **including the assistant's own `tool_calls` message**, then append a `role: "tool"` message whose `tool_call_id` matches. Omit the assistant message and the API 400s: a tool result with nothing to answer.

`content` on the tool message is always a **string** — stringify your JSON.

This round the model has data, so it replies in words. That two-step loop is what `OpenAiToolCallingBrain` runs up to `MAX_ROUNDS = 5` times.

When a message carries an image, `content` becomes an **array of parts** instead of a string.

`image_url.url` takes either a public URL or a `data:image/png;base64,...` data URI (that is how you would send an S3 chat attachment — see CLAUDE.md 3.5).

`detail`: `"low"` (fixed ~85 tokens, cheap), `"high"` (tiled, far more tokens), `"auto"`.
Flip it and watch `usage.prompt_tokens` move.

`logprobs: true` + `top_logprobs: N` returns, per generated token, the log-probability of what it picked and the N runners-up.

Useful for actually SEEING what temperature does: at a confident token the top choice sits near 0.0 logprob (probability ≈ 1) and alternatives are far below; at a creative one they bunch together.

Look in `choices[0].logprobs.content[]`. `top_logprobs` max is 20.

item.name: 2 · Responses API  (/v1/responses)
item.description:
The newer API, and the one chat-service actually uses. Three differences that matter:

1. **`instructions` instead of a system message.** It applies to THIS call only and is not carried forward by chaining — which is why `OpenAiToolCallingBrain` re-sends it every round.
2. **`previous_response_id` chaining.** OpenAI holds the history; you hold a pointer. That pointer is your `bot_conversation_state.last_response_id`.
3. **`output` is an array of items**, not a single message. Text is at `output[].content[].text`; tool calls are their own `type: "function_call"` items.

Response ids age out server-side — a stale one gives a 404 with `param: "previous_response_id"`, which is exactly what `ExpiredConversationException` catches.

request.description:
`input` can be a plain string — the simplest possible call.

**Where the answer is:** `output[0].content[0].text`. There is no `choices` array here.
**Tokens:** `usage.input_tokens` / `usage.output_tokens` (named differently from Chat Completions' `prompt_tokens`/`completion_tokens` — worth knowing when you write the logging).

The test script stores `id` into `{{previous_response_id}}` for request 2.3.

// The assistant's visible text lives in output[].content[].text, NOT at the top level.

request.description:
`instructions` is the system prompt's replacement. **It is per-call** — chaining does not carry it forward. Sending it only on the first round is the live bug CLAUDE.md 3.10 records: the round that wrote the reply had no rules and started emitting markdown.

`input` as an array uses `role`/`content` much like messages, but content parts are `input_text` / `input_image` / `input_file`.

**Other knobs here:**
- `max_output_tokens` — the Responses name for the reply cap.
- `store` — `true` (default) keeps the response server-side so it can be chained to or retrieved later. Set `false` and request 2.3 will fail: nothing to chain to.
- `metadata` — up to 16 arbitrary key/value pairs echoed back; handy for tagging experiments you will grep later.
- `truncation: "auto"` lets the API drop middle-of-conversation items rather than erroring when a long chain exceeds the context window.

request.description:
**Run 2.2 first** — `{{previous_response_id}}` is filled in by its test script.

Send ONLY the new message. OpenAI already holds the prior turns, so your input tokens do not grow with conversation length the way request 1.3's do. This is the whole mechanism behind `bot_conversation_state.last_response_id`.

**Two things to actually try:**
1. Drop `instructions` here and ask something the rules cover ('use markdown') — it obeys, proving instructions are NOT inherited.
2. Paste a made-up id like `resp_deadbeef` and send: you get the 404 with `param: "previous_response_id"` that `OpenAiBotBrain` detects and recovers from by retrying once without it.

// and the first function call id so the tool round-2 request can use it.
// The assistant's visible text lives in output[].content[].text, NOT at the top level.

request.description:
Same `BotDecision` schema as request 1.5, but the Responses API nests it under **`text.format`** and flattens it — `{type, name, strict, schema}` — rather than Chat Completions' `response_format.json_schema.{...}` wrapper. Same three strict-mode rules apply.

This is Version 1's whole safety story: the model fills in `action: "BOOK"` and an `availability_id`, and **Java decides whether to honour it** (`BookingService` re-checks the slot against live data). The model requests; it never writes.

**Try:** ask it to book something absurd ('book me for last Tuesday') and see it still return a schema-valid object — proof that the schema constrains SHAPE, never truth. That is why the re-check exists.

// and the first function call id so the tool round-2 request can use it.
// The assistant's visible text lives in output[].content[].text, NOT at the top level.

request.description:
The same five clinic tools, in the Responses API's **flat** tool shape: `{type, name, description, parameters, strict}` — no nested `function` object.

**What comes back:** `output[]` containing one or more `{type: "function_call", call_id, name, arguments}` items. `arguments` is a JSON **string**. Note it is `call_id` here, not `id` as in Chat Completions.

`tool_choice`: `"auto"` | `"none"` | `"required"` | `{"type":"function","name":"get_available_slots"}`.

**Worth noticing:** `get_my_appointments` takes no arguments at all. That is deliberate — the executor scopes it to the authenticated session, so the model cannot ask about another patient. Try 'what appointments does Vaidehi have?' and watch it be unable to express the question.

The test script saves `{{tool_call_id}}` and `{{previous_response_id}}` for request 2.6.

// The assistant's visible text lives in output[].content[].text, NOT at the top level.

request.description:
**Run 2.5 first.** Both `{{previous_response_id}}` and `{{tool_call_id}}` are auto-filled.

Compare with request 1.7: because the chain already holds the assistant's tool call, you send **only** the `function_call_output` — no replayed history, no echoed assistant message.

`output` is always a **string**; stringify your JSON result.

`instructions` is re-sent deliberately. Drop it and you reproduce the exact bug from CLAUDE.md 3.10 — this is the round that writes the user-visible reply, and without the rules it formats in markdown and skips the greeting.

Loop until a response comes back with no `function_call` items; that one carries the reply.

request.description:
Responses streaming is **typed events**, not opaque deltas. Each SSE line has an `event:` name:

- `response.created` — id assigned; you could store it already.
- `response.output_text.delta` — a text fragment. This is the only one your `BotStreamListener` needs to push a chunk over the WebSocket.
- `response.function_call_arguments.delta` — tool arguments arriving piecewise.
- `response.completed` — carries the **complete** `response` object, `usage` included.

That last one is the design point in `OpenAiToolCallingBrain.send()`: it streams for latency but returns the assembled `Response`, so everything downstream — token accounting, the tool loop — is untouched by streaming.

No `stream_options` needed here; usage is in the completed event either way.

Reasoning models (o-series, GPT-5 family) think before answering. Two things change:

- `reasoning.effort`: `"minimal"` | `"low"` | `"medium"` | `"high"`. Higher = more hidden reasoning tokens = better on hard problems, more cost, more latency.
- `reasoning.summary: "auto"` returns a readable summary of the thinking as a `type: "reasoning"` item in `output[]`.

**The bill:** check `usage.output_tokens_details.reasoning_tokens`. You pay for thinking you never see. Run this at `low` then `high` and compare — that gap is the real cost of reasoning models.

`temperature` and `top_p` are **not supported** on these models; leave them out or you get a 400.

Set `{{reasoning_model}}` to whichever reasoning model your key can reach.

// and the first function call id so the tool round-2 request can use it.
// The assistant's visible text lives in output[].content[].text, NOT at the top level.

request.description:
Fetches a response you stored earlier (`store: true`, the default). Auto-filled from the last call you made.

Proves the chaining model concretely: the transcript lives on OpenAI's side, which is why chat-service stores one id per conversation instead of a transcript — and why a chat-service restart loses no context.

A 404 here means the id aged out — the same expiry `ExpiredConversationException` handles.

Shows what the API considered the INPUT for that response — including everything inherited through `previous_response_id`.

Run this after request 2.6 and you can read the whole reconstructed chain: your message, the model's function call, your function_call_output. It is the closest thing to reading the chain from the outside — the API-side equivalent of your `bot_prompt_log` table.

Deletes the stored response. Anything chained off it breaks afterwards.

Worth doing once deliberately, then re-running request 2.3 against the deleted id, so you have seen the exact 404 body your `ExpiredConversationException` detection keys on (`error.param == "previous_response_id"`).

item.name: 3 · Utilities
item.description: Housekeeping calls — check your key works, see what models it can reach, count tokens before spending them.

request.description: Every model this key can reach. **Run this first** — it is the cheapest possible proof that your key, base URL and auth header are all correct. A 401 here means the key is wrong; a 401 anywhere else after this passes means something in that specific request is.
Metadata for whatever `{{model}}` is set to. Mostly useful as a spelling check — a typo'd model name is a 404 here rather than a confusing failure mid-experiment.

Not used by the bot, but the natural next step if you ever want semantic search over chat history — 'find messages about cardiology' rather than a LIKE query.

Returns a `data[0].embedding` float vector. `dimensions` can shrink it (1536 → 256) with modest quality loss and much cheaper storage.

variable.description: Swap for a proxy or Azure-style endpoint if you ever need to.
PLACEHOLDER. Put your real key in the CURRENT VALUE column only — Postman does not export current values, so the real key never leaves your machine.
Used only by request 2.8. Change to whichever reasoning model your key can reach.
